title: Ready to Learn: Notice, Think, Explain
subject: routines

blocks.title: Welcome, class.
lines: Sit in your place.
Put your bag under your desk.
Think about the question.

blocks.title: What helps you learn?
lines: Choose one. Be ready to explain.
blocks.footnote: Different answers are welcome.

blocks.title: Start the task, or ask for help.
lines: You do not have to get every answer right.

blocks.title: Tell your partner one thing that helps you learn.
lines: Take turns.

blocks.title: When the signal appears:
lines: Finish your sentence.
Pause.
Listen.

blocks.title: When the signal appears:
lines: Finish your sentence.
Pause.
Listen.

blocks.title: Observation
lines: What the picture shows.
There is a puddle.

blocks.title: Inference
lines: A possible explanation.
It may have rained.

blocks.title: An inference needs evidence.
lines: It might still be wrong.

blocks.title: Could the puddle have another explanation?
Someone may have spilled water.
lines: That is another possible explanation.

blocks.title: Find two things you can see.
lines: I can see…

blocks.title: Share your observations.
lines: Suggest one possible explanation.
I think… because…

blocks.title: Do we see it, or are we explaining it?
lines: One person speaks.
Others listen.

blocks.title: What is the mistake?
lines: “There is a puddle, so it definitely rained.”

blocks.title: Rain is only one possible explanation.
One possible response
lines: Other sensible explanations are welcome.
There is a puddle. It may have rained, but the water could have come from somewhere else.

blocks.title: One observation I made was…
lines: Think first. Then share when invited.

We can see the umbrella, but we do not know why it is there.

questions.prompt: There are no people in the picture.

An empty picture does not prove that the school is closed.

sections.title: Prepare with a short revision routine

blocks.title: Retrieval beats rereading
lines: Read the notes from your recent lessons. Close them and explain three ideas from memory.
Practise a question, check the explanation, and correct your reasoning.
Revisit the topics you found difficult tomorrow.
This is revision practice from teaching lessons, not an assessment paper or an answer key.

title: From product to global supply chain
subject: global-perspectives

blocks.title: Follow a T-shirt
lines: Write the four stages in order. Use the picture to check.
Tell your partner which stage needs fabric, and why.
1. Country A: grow cotton. A farmer needs water and land.
2. Country B: weave fabric. A weaver needs cotton and a loom.
3. Country C: sew the shirt. A garment worker needs fabric and a sewing machine.
4. Country D: sell the shirt. A shop worker needs finished shirts and a shop.

blocks.title: Build an explanation
lines: A supply chain links stages of production, not just places on a map.
Say: “I think … because the source says … But we do not know …”

blocks.title: Explain one connection
lines: The garment worker in C needs fabric from B to sew a shirt.
Without fabric, sewing may have to wait. “May” shows a possible effect, not a proven fact.
Now explain a different link yourself. Your partner points to the evidence.
1. Country A: grow cotton. A farmer needs water and land.
2. Country B: weave fabric. A weaver needs cotton and a loom.
3. Country C: sew the shirt. A garment worker needs fabric and a sewing machine.
4. Country D: sell the shirt. A shop worker needs finished shirts and a shop.

lines: A farmer plants trees to shelter crops. Which explanation connects people and nature?
Write or say one sentence independently.
What is here? Where is it?
Physical: river, hill, soil.
blocks.imageAlt: Illustrated imaginary coastal town, countryside and transport links.
blocks.imageCaption: Imagined teaching illustration • use the lesson source for exact facts.

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Examples: a mountain is a physical feature; a road is human-made; pollution in a river links human activity and the environment.
questions.model: A mountain is a natural landform.

lines: A farmer plants trees to shelter crops. Which explanation connects people and nature?
Give one short answer when invited.
A reservoir contains water, but a dam built by people changes its storage. Name the natural feature, the human action and the effect; do not force every example into one box.
questions.model: People change vegetation to reduce wind exposure. Vegetation is natural material; planting and shelter are human action and purpose.

lines: Explain one possible connection between them.
Fictional field sketch: a wooded slope beside a footpath. Proposed change: trees are removed beside the path. No before-and-after measurements have been made.
questions.model: trees are removed beside the path may lead to less shade and exposed soil. This is a prediction, not a measured result.

lines: What could we observe to test the prediction?
Fictional field sketch: a wooded slope beside a footpath. Proposed change: trees are removed beside the path. No before-and-after measurements have been made.
questions.model: Compare the affected area with a similar unchanged area; measure the predicted effect at comparable times.

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Examples: a mountain is a physical feature; a road is human-made; pollution in a river links human activity and the environment.
questions.model: Roads are constructed by people.

questions.prompt: Which resource helps locate a country?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
An atlas helps locate places; a compass indicates directions; a ruler measures a line; a photograph records a visible scene.
questions.model: An atlas contains maps.

lines: Which label could guide a real school investigation?
Give one short answer when invited.
An exhibit label needs more than a name. “Shaded bench: built seat beneath a tree; is it cooler here at noon?” identifies a feature, a connection and a question that measurements could answer.
questions.model: Paved path: does rainwater remain longer here than on soil? The first names comparable surfaces and an observable outcome; the second supplies an unsupported judgement.

lines: You need to locate Peru within a continent. Which resource helps directly?
Give one short answer when invited.

A photograph can show a path but its perspective distorts length. For distance, use a measured map line and a scale; for direction, use a north arrow or compass. State what each tool can and cannot tell you.
questions.model: An atlas index and map. The index locates the country; a ruler measures length but does not identify countries.

lines: Explain one possible connection between them.

questions.prompt: Which tool measures a line on paper?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Examples: a mountain is a physical feature; a road is human-made; pollution in a river links human activity and the environment.
questions.model: Roads are constructed by people.

questions.prompt: Which tool measures a line on paper?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
An atlas helps locate places; a compass indicates directions; a ruler measures a line; a photograph records a visible scene.
questions.model: A ruler measures paper lengths.

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Fictional school log: 8 pupils waited at Door A and 2 at Door B at 12:00. The observer did not ask why.

options.label: Eight pupils waited at Door A.

questions.model: Only the count and time were recorded.

lines: Which label could guide a real school investigation?
Give one short answer when invited.
An exhibit label needs more than a name. “Shaded bench: built seat beneath a tree; is it cooler here at noon?” identifies a feature, a connection and a question that measurements could answer.
questions.model: Paved path: does rainwater remain longer here than on soil? The first names comparable surfaces and an observable outcome; the second supplies an unsupported judgement.

lines: Which field note is checkable?
Give one short answer when invited.
A useful record says “line B, 4 cm, measured from the zero mark”. “It is four” leaves the object and unit unknown. For an observation, record what is visible separately from a suggested cause.
questions.model: At 10:00, three bags were beside the west wall. Time, count and location let someone repeat the observation; popularity needs other evidence.

lines: A queue is longer at Gate X. What can a single count establish?
Give one short answer when invited.
If one gate has 9 people and another has 3, the difference is 6. This establishes a count, not why people chose the gate. Turn a suggested reason into a question you could investigate.
questions.model: More people were waiting there at that moment. A snapshot describes a moment; repeated timing would be needed to compare service.

lines: Explain one possible connection between them.
Fictional field sketch: a river bank beside a car park. Proposed change: the bank is paved. No before-and-after measurements have been made.
questions.model: the bank is paved may lead to less water can soak into that surface. This is a prediction, not a measured result.

lines: Calculate the represented distance together.
Equipment bench: a map line measures 12 cm; its scale is 1 cm = 110 m. A broken ruler still has marks 11 cm and 23 cm. North is at the top of the map.
questions.model: 12 × 110 = 1320 m. Invite one pupil to choose the operation and another to check the units.

questions.prompt: Which river does the Iron Bridge cross?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
The Iron Bridge crosses the River Severn. It was completed in 1779 and opened to traffic in 1781. A bridge can change connections between river banks.
questions.model: The verified source identifies the Severn.

lines: A bag lies on a zone boundary. What should the team do?
Give one short answer when invited.
Choose two zones, define what counts, record the same length of time and repeat. A bag touching a boundary needs a rule agreed before counting. Report “our two zones”, not “the whole school”.
questions.model: Apply the agreed boundary rule once. A shared rule prevents double counting and inconsistent results.

lines: An imagined bridge opens. Which claim needs additional evidence?
Give one short answer when invited.

A ferry carries people across in batches; a bridge provides a fixed connection when open. This suggests an access mechanism, but does not prove how many jobs were created. Label historical facts separately from predictions in a model.
questions.model: Local trade increased by 50%. A precise economic change requires records; it cannot be read from the crossing symbol.

lines: How much did the count change from 09:00 to 09:05?
Fictional queue count: at 09:00, 7 people; at 09:05, 12; at 09:10, 9. Observer A counts people waiting inside the barrier. Observer B also counts people walking past.
questions.model: It increased by 5. The subtraction compares the two counts.

lines: Name something that stayed the same.

Fictional before/after panels: BEFORE — a ferry and two farms. AFTER — a bridge, three homes and a workshop. Both panels cover the same area. river and hill remain. There are no traffic or sales measurements.
questions.model: river and hill. Change is not the same as complete replacement.

lines: Does the highest queue count prove slow service?
Fictional queue count: at 09:00, 7 people; at 09:05, 12; at 09:10, 9. Observer A counts people waiting inside the barrier. Observer B also counts people walking past.
questions.model: No. More arrivals can also enlarge a queue. Measure arrivals and service times before explaining the cause.

lines: “Everyone became richer.” Can the panels support that?

Fictional before/after panels: BEFORE — a ferry and two farms. AFTER — a bridge, three homes and a workshop. Both panels cover the same area. river and hill remain. There are no traffic or sales measurements.
questions.model: No. Buildings do not show everyone’s income. Income or employment evidence would be needed.

questions.prompt: Which possible effect needs additional evidence?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
The Iron Bridge crosses the River Severn. It was completed in 1779 and opened to traffic in 1781. A bridge can change connections between river banks.

options.label: The exact change in traders' incomes.
The river's name in the source.

questions.model: The source dates do not measure income effects.

lines: A river remains in both drawings while a workshop appears. What belongs in the changed column?
Give one short answer when invited.

Make rows for crossing, buildings and land cover, then columns for before and after. Compare each feature with itself. “Three buildings replace one” is an observation; “families were happier” is not visible evidence.
questions.model: The workshop appeared. Match the same feature across the two sources before describing change.

lines: What would weaken the claim that the walkway caused a stall to open?
Give one short answer when invited.

A crossing may improve access to a workshop; a new walkway may bring customers past a stall. The shared mechanism is access, while business type and context differ. Compare opening dates and customer counts to test it.
questions.model: Records show the stall opened five years earlier. An earlier opening cannot be caused by a later walkway; proximity alone is weak evidence.

lines: Name something that stayed the same.

Fictional before/after panels: BEFORE — a long riverside detour and a shop. AFTER — a footbridge and three stalls. Both panels cover the same area. river bend and old shop remain. There are no traffic or sales measurements.
questions.model: river bend and old shop. Change is not the same as complete replacement.

lines: Name something that stayed the same.

Fictional before/after panels: BEFORE — a narrow road and a field. AFTER — a wider road and a warehouse. Both panels cover the same area. field boundary and stream remain. There are no traffic or sales measurements.
questions.model: field boundary and stream. Change is not the same as complete replacement.

lines: “Everyone became richer.” Can the panels support that?

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Imagined routes: A is 400 m with stairs; B is 600 m with a ramp. A traveller uses a wheelchair.
Which missing detail matters most to whether a ramp can be used?
Give one short answer when invited.

A 300 m staircase route is shorter than a 500 m ramp route. For a wheelchair user, usable access is a constraint, while distance is a preference after access is checked. A ramp still needs a suitable gradient and condition.
questions.model: Its gradient and surface condition. Access labels alone do not establish practical usability.

lines: Two users choose different routes. What is the strongest comparison?
Give one short answer when invited.

A walker who can use stairs may prioritise time; someone carrying a heavy trolley may prioritise surface and slope. Keep the routes constant while changing the traveller to see why one universal “best” answer fails.
questions.model: Check each user's needs against the same route evidence. Different priorities can justify different choices from the same evidence.

lines: Which route would you investigate first for the wheelchair user?

Fictional routes: A is 250 m with stairs; B is 450 m with a ramp. Both are open. First traveller: a wheelchair user. Second traveller: a walker carrying a light bag. Ramp condition has not been checked.
questions.model: B, because it has a ramp. Check gradient, width and surface before calling it accessible.

questions.prompt: Which map is more relevant to a 2026 bus journey?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Map A is a simplified 1900 town sketch showing a river and bridge. Map B is a 2026 route map showing roads and bus stops. Both are classroom inventions.

options.label: A solely because it is older
Neither because all maps are identical
The map with no route information

questions.model: B contains current route-related features in the example.

lines: The shorter bridge is closed. Which action comes first?
Give one short answer when invited.

A closed path is not an option today even if its recorded length is shortest. Cross unavailable choices out before ranking what remains. A recommendation needs both a route and the conditions under which it works.
questions.model: Find an open crossing before comparing journey lengths. A measured advantage cannot override an unavailable connection.

lines: Which map would best investigate former mills?
Give one short answer when invited.
A factory map from the past can locate former industry; a current transport map can show bus connections. Detail is selected for a purpose. Older does not automatically mean useless.
questions.model: A dated historical land-use map. Historical land use directly addresses former industry, though its date and coverage still matter.

lines: Which route would you investigate first for the wheelchair user?

Fictional routes: A is 350 m with stairs; B is 550 m with a ramp. Both are open. First traveller: a wheelchair user. Second traveller: a walker carrying a light bag. Ramp condition has not been checked.
questions.model: B, because it has a ramp. Check gradient, width and surface before calling it accessible.

lines: Which map helps plan the bus connection?
Map A is a 1910 mill map. Map B is a current bus-route map with stops and connections, but no small paths. A visitor wants to investigate former industry, then travel by bus.
questions.model: B: routes and stops match that purpose. A current map still does not prove a service is running now.

lines: New report: A is closed. What changes?

Fictional routes: A is 350 m with stairs; B is 550 m with a ramp. Both are open. First traveller: a wheelchair user. Second traveller: a walker carrying a light bag. Ramp condition has not been checked.
questions.model: A is unavailable regardless of length. Reconsider the open route or another open crossing.

lines: Name one useful piece of information missing from B.
Map A is a 1910 mill map. Map B is a current bus-route map with stops and connections, but no small paths. A visitor wants to investigate former industry, then travel by bus.
questions.model: For a journey: service times, disruption or step-free access. Explain the user’s need.

lines: Which feature is most useful on a map for a new wheelchair user?
Give one short answer when invited.

A walking map needs paths, crossings and entrances; a bus map needs stops and route connections. Both omit detail so users can find the relevant information. Explain each inclusion in terms of the user's job.
questions.model: Step-free entrances. The user's access question determines which detail is necessary.

lines: A park path is absent on a national road map. What follows?
Give one short answer when invited.
A small path may be missing because of scale, date or map purpose. Before calling it new, compare maps with similar coverage and check a dated source. “Not shown” is the observation.
questions.model: The map may omit small paths. Selection and scale provide alternative explanations for omission.

lines: Which map helps plan the bus connection?
Map A is a 1950 field map. Map B is a current bus-route map with stops and connections, but no small paths. A visitor wants to investigate former land use, then travel by bus.
questions.model: B: routes and stops match that purpose. A current map still does not prove a service is running now.

blocks.title: Mistake clinic · Diagnose a scale calculation rather than guess · your task
lines: Station 1: Find the error in the proposed answer.
Replace it, explain the misconception and write a clue that would help another pupil avoid it.

questions.prompt: How long is 8 m on the plan?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Practice plan: 1 cm represents 20 m. A classroom is 8 m by 6 m. A path is drawn 3 cm long.
Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Two fictional pupils draw the same route. One includes a shop, the other a playground. Neither measures distances.

options.label: That a shop can be a landmark.

questions.model: No measurements or scale were used.

questions.prompt: Where is the pond relative to the school?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented scene: a school in the west, a pond in the east, a road across the south and a park in the north. North is at the top.
questions.model: The scene places the pond east of the school.

lines: At 1 cm = 20 m, what drawing length represents 60 m?
Give one short answer when invited.
At 1 cm = 25 m, 75 m needs 3 cm, not 75 cm. Write one conversion for every feature; all features on the plan share the same scale. A doorway cannot use a different conversion.
questions.model: 3 cm. Divide 60 by 20 when going from ground distance to map length.

lines: A visitor needs a route tomorrow. What should be checked first?
Give one short answer when invited.

Draw uncertain turns with a question mark. Check direction, crossing access and distances against observations or a reliable map. A draft becomes useful when uncertainty is visible rather than hidden.
questions.model: An uncertain turn and whether the crossing is open. Uncertainty at a decision point can change whether the visitor reaches the destination.

lines: A pond is west of a building. What must survive simplification?
Give one short answer when invited.
A roof becomes a building symbol; a pond becomes an area symbol. Preserve relative position while simplifying shape. A key explains meaning; a north arrow explains orientation.
questions.model: The pond remains west of the building. A useful plan preserves spatial relationships while omitting unnecessary detail.

lines: Give the room’s two drawing dimensions.
Fictional room: 132 m long and 88 m wide. Doorway: 22 m. Drawing scale: 1 cm = 22 m. Available drawing space: 8 cm × 6 cm. Use the board, not a ruler on the screen.
questions.model: 132 ÷ 22 = 6 cm; 88 ÷ 22 = 4 cm. Label drawing and real units separately.

lines: Which landmark tells you where to turn?
Remember this fictional route: market → clock → turn left at clinic → crossing → station. No distances or starting compass direction are supplied.
questions.model: clinic. It is a decision point, not merely decoration.

lines: Choose a symbol for each feature and say its meaning.
Fictional aerial view, north at the top: school west; pond east; park north; road south. The map maker proposes simple shapes instead of detailed pictures.
questions.model: Accept four distinct, simple symbols and a key that matches the drawing.

lines: Will this drawing fit? Explain using both dimensions.
Fictional room: 132 m long and 88 m wide. Doorway: 22 m. Drawing scale: 1 cm = 22 m. Available drawing space: 8 cm × 6 cm. Use the board, not a ruler on the screen.
questions.model: Yes: 6 cm ≤ 8 cm and 4 cm ≤ 6 cm.

lines: A pupil draws equal gaps. Does that prove equal distances?
Remember this fictional route: market → clock → turn left at clinic → crossing → station. No distances or starting compass direction are supplied.
questions.model: No. A memory sequence is not a measured scale map.

lines: The key calls a blue circle “pond”, but the plan uses it for school. Repair it.

questions.prompt: What is the tree's four-figure reference?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Practice grid: a tree is in square 2345, 6 tenths across and 2 tenths up. Draw eastings 23–25 and northings 45–47.
questions.model: Use the square's easting 23 then northing 45.

lines: Which omitted detail could prevent a visitor finding reception?
Give one short answer when invited.
A visitor needs gate, reception, path connections and a clear destination. Furniture inside unrelated rooms adds clutter. Test the map by asking someone to trace the route using only its information.
questions.model: The entrance connecting the street to the path. A broken route connection matters more than unrelated interior detail.

lines: What is the six-figure reference for 2 across and 8 up in 2345?
Give one short answer when invited.
For square 2345, 23 is the left easting and 45 the bottom northing. A point 4 tenths across and 7 up becomes 234457: join 23+4, then 45+7. Four figures identify a square, six refine the position.
questions.model: 232458. Keep the easting and its tenths together before writing the northing and its tenths.

lines: Choose a symbol for each feature and say its meaning.
Fictional aerial view, north at the top: library west; sports field east; garden north; bus stop south. The map maker proposes simple shapes instead of detailed pictures.
questions.model: Accept four distinct, simple symbols and a key that matches the drawing.

lines: Build A’s six-figure reference one half at a time.
Practice grid square 2345. Rescue point A is 2 tenths east and 7 tenths north within the square. Point B is 4 tenths east and 5 tenths north.
questions.model: 232457: easting plus tenths, then northing plus tenths.

lines: The key calls a blue circle “pond”, but the plan uses it for school. Repair it.
Fictional aerial view, north at the top: library west; sports field east; garden north; bus stop south. The map maker proposes simple shapes instead of detailed pictures.
questions.model: Change the key or the symbol consistently. The same symbol must keep the same meaning.

lines: Which point is farther north?
Practice grid square 2345. Rescue point A is 2 tenths east and 7 tenths north within the square. Point B is 4 tenths east and 5 tenths north.
questions.model: A, because 7 is greater than 5 tenths up.

cards.back:
A photograph records visible detail.
A plan shows positions using simpler shapes.

Use north, east, south and west.
Look for neighbouring features.

One symbol has one meaning.
Use distinct symbols for different features.

A plan can show arrangement.
It may not show height or current use.
The key gives the symbol's meaning.

questions.prompt: How much longer is the route?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Practice map scale: 1 cm = 100 m. A straight line is 4 cm; a route has segments 2 cm, 3 cm and 1 cm.
Choose an answer. Explain your reason.

questions.model: 25,000 cm equals 250 m.

lines: A 200 m route grows from 2 cm to 4 cm on a copy. What is the new scale?
Give one short answer when invited.

A 3 cm line representing 300 m becomes 6 cm after doubling the print. The real route stays 300 m, so 1 cm now represents 50 m. A scale bar resized with the map still represents the same real distance.
questions.model: 1 cm = 50 m. Divide the unchanged 200 m by the new 4 cm length.

lines: At 1:25,000, what does 4 cm represent?
Give one short answer when invited.
At 1:25,000, 1 cm represents 25,000 cm. Since 100 cm is 1 m, that is 250 m. Decode the map key before treating a line as a road, stream or footpath.
Convert A and B to real distances.

questions.prompt: Which point is at the Equator and prime meridian intersection?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented points: A 20°N, 30°E; B 20°S, 30°E; C 0°, 0°. These are coordinate exercises, not named cities.
questions.model: Both coordinates are zero.

lines: Which quadrant contains 15°N, 25°W?
Give one short answer when invited.
The Equator divides north from south; the prime meridian divides east from west for longitude. Write latitude first. 10°S, 20°E means south of the Equator and east of the prime meridian.
questions.model: North-west of the zero-line intersection. N belongs to latitude; W belongs to longitude.

lines: Move 12°S, 40°E to the opposite longitude hemisphere, keeping latitude. What changes?
Give one short answer when invited.
A west longitude cannot be plotted east of the prime meridian. Read the direction letters before plotting numbers; changing E to W changes hemisphere even when the number stays 30.
questions.model: It becomes 12°S, 40°W. Keep latitude fixed and change only east to west.

lines: Which two points share longitude?
Coordinate sketch: A 15°N, 25°E; B 15°S, 25°E; C 15°N, 25°W. Equator = 0° latitude; prime meridian = 0° longitude.
questions.model: A and B: both 25°E, but their latitudes differ.

lines: Which two points share longitude?
Coordinate sketch: A 20°N, 30°E; B 20°S, 30°E; C 20°N, 30°W. Equator = 0° latitude; prime meridian = 0° longitude.
questions.model: A and B: both 30°E, but their latitudes differ.

lines: Move A to the opposite side of the prime meridian, keeping latitude.
Coordinate sketch: A 15°N, 25°E; B 15°S, 25°E; C 15°N, 25°W. Equator = 0° latitude; prime meridian = 0° longitude.
questions.model: It becomes 15°N, 25°W: the location of C.

lines: Move A to the opposite side of the prime meridian, keeping latitude.
Coordinate sketch: A 20°N, 30°E; B 20°S, 30°E; C 20°N, 30°W. Equator = 0° latitude; prime meridian = 0° longitude.
questions.model: It becomes 20°N, 30°W: the location of C.

lines: Station 2: Prepare a three-step explanation for someone who missed the lesson.
Include an example, a common wrong turn and a check.
Partners follow the steps and report any gap.

Review case: Can the lower hill have the steeper side? Proposed answer: “No, the highest summit always has the steepest slope.”. Method note: A 60 m rise over 100 m is steeper than a 120 m rise over 600 m: 0.6 versus 0.2 rise/run. Compare ratios, not just the larger height. Contour spacing comparisons also need equal scales and intervals.

questions.prompt: How long is the 2 cm path?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Practice extract description: scale 1:25,000; a path is 2 cm long. Its key identifies P as parking and a blue line as a stream. This is an original exercise, not an OS extract.

questions.prompt: What is the total height gain?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Practice cross-section at 100 m spacing: heights 100, 120, 160, 180 m. A second slope rises 20 m over 100 m.

questions.prompt: Which point is south of the Equator?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented points: A 20°N, 30°E; B 20°S, 30°E; C 0°, 0°. These are coordinate exercises, not named cities.
questions.model: B has latitude 20°S.

lines: Which usually allows more detail for a local walk?
Give one short answer when invited.
At 1:25,000, 2 cm is 500 m; at 1:250,000 it is 5 km. The latter covers more ground in the same page space, leaving less room for local detail. A larger denominator means a smaller map scale.
questions.model: 1:25,000. More paper space is available per unit of ground distance at 1:25,000.

lines: Can the lower hill have the steeper side?
Give one short answer when invited.
A 60 m rise over 100 m is steeper than a 120 m rise over 600 m: 0.6 versus 0.2 rise/run. Compare ratios, not just the larger height. Contour spacing comparisons also need equal scales and intervals.
questions.model: Yes, if height increases more quickly over horizontal distance. Elevation and gradient measure different things.

lines: Which quadrant contains 15°N, 25°W?
Give one short answer when invited.
The Equator divides north from south; the prime meridian divides east from west for longitude. Write latitude first. 10°S, 20°E means south of the Equator and east of the prime meridian.
questions.model: North-west of the zero-line intersection. N belongs to latitude; W belongs to longitude.

lines: What ground distance does 1 cm represent on A?
Original classroom map key: P = parking, blue line = stream, dashed line = footpath. Map A scale 1:25,000; Map B scale 1:250,000. A dashed route measures 28 cm on A and crosses a stream.
questions.model: 25,000 cm = 250 m. Convert centimetres to metres.

lines: Find the rise in each interval.
Fictional profile points: distance 0, 100, 200, 300 m; height 350, 360, 400, 420 m. All horizontal intervals are equal. North is irrelevant to this height comparison.
questions.model: 10 m, 40 m and 20 m, each over 100 m horizontally.

lines: Which two points share longitude?
Coordinate sketch: A 15°N, 45°E; B 15°S, 45°E; C 15°N, 45°W. Equator = 0° latitude; prime meridian = 0° longitude.
questions.model: A and B: both 45°E, but their latitudes differ.

lines: The same drawn length on B represents what distance?
Original classroom map key: P = parking, blue line = stream, dashed line = footpath. Map A scale 1:25,000; Map B scale 1:250,000. A dashed route measures 28 cm on A and crosses a stream.
questions.model: 28 × 2,500 = 70000 m, ten times as far.

lines: What is the total rise from first to last point?
Fictional profile points: distance 0, 100, 200, 300 m; height 350, 360, 400, 420 m. All horizontal intervals are equal. North is irrelevant to this height comparison.
questions.model: 70 m. Subtract the first height from the last.

lines: Move A to the opposite side of the prime meridian, keeping latitude.
Coordinate sketch: A 15°N, 45°E; B 15°S, 45°E; C 15°N, 45°W. Equator = 0° latitude; prime meridian = 0° longitude.
questions.model: It becomes 15°N, 45°W: the location of C.

questions.prompt: Which country is in the UK but not on Great Britain?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
The UK is off north-west mainland Europe. The North Sea is east, the Atlantic west and the English Channel south. Great Britain contains England, Scotland and Wales.
questions.model: Northern Ireland is on the island of Ireland.

questions.prompt: Which station was warmer that day?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented one-day readings: West station 12°C and 18 mm rain; East station 14°C and 4 mm. In the UK, west-facing high ground often receives more rain.
questions.model: 14°C is warmer than 12°C.

lines: Which statement places Northern Ireland correctly?
Give one short answer when invited.

Great Britain is the island containing England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland is on the island of Ireland and is also part of the UK. Start with the islands, then add country names and surrounding waters.
questions.model: Part of the UK, on the island of Ireland. Political membership and island location are different kinds of information.

lines: The incoming air becomes much drier. What prediction follows, other things equal?
Give one short answer when invited.

Moist air rises over high ground and cools. Condensation can form cloud and precipitation. Descending air on the other side may be drier; wind and moisture supply matter, so a mountain does not guarantee rain every day.

lines: The incoming air becomes much drier. What prediction follows, other things equal?

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
The UK is off north-west mainland Europe. The North Sea is east, the Atlantic west and the English Channel south. Great Britain contains England, Scotland and Wales.
questions.model: The North Sea lies between Great Britain and northern mainland Europe.

questions.prompt: Which belongs on a political map?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
The Scottish Highlands are in northern Great Britain; Wales is west of England. A country boundary is different from a mountain range.
questions.model: Political maps represent territorial divisions.

questions.prompt: How much more rain fell at West?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented one-day readings: West station 12°C and 18 mm rain; East station 14°C and 4 mm. In the UK, west-facing high ground often receives more rain.
questions.model: 18 minus 4 is 14 mm.

questions.prompt: Which station was warmer that day?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented one-day readings: West station 12°C and 18 mm rain; East station 14°C and 4 mm. In the UK, west-facing high ground often receives more rain.
questions.model: 14°C is warmer than 12°C.

questions.prompt: How many respondents enjoy both activities?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented town survey: 12 people enjoy football, 8 enjoy music and 5 enjoy both. These are separate overlapping groups, not national statistics.

lines: Which two features are physical?
Map layers: country boundary for Wales; approximate upland area labelled Scottish Highlands; river line labelled Thames. A city point is also marked. Colours and symbols are explained in the key.
questions.model: Scottish Highlands and Thames: relief and a river, rather than a country boundary.

lines: Which station is wetter, and by how much?
Fictional weather on one day: West station 20°C and 24 mm rain; East station 23°C and 2 mm rain. A mountain stands between them. Incoming air is moist and blows from the west.
questions.model: West has 22 mm more rain that day.

lines: How many like walking, including those who like both?
Fictional club survey: 17 pupils like walking only, 13 like cycling only, 14 like both. Everyone surveyed likes at least one. The survey was conducted at an outdoor club.
questions.model: 17+14=31. “Walking” is not the same as “walking only”.

lines: Which layer would help investigate high land?
Map layers: country boundary for Wales; approximate upland area labelled Scottish Highlands; river line labelled Thames. A city point is also marked. Colours and symbols are explained in the key.

questions.prompt: Which belongs on a political map?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
The Scottish Highlands are in northern Great Britain; Wales is west of England. A country boundary is different from a mountain range.
questions.model: Political maps represent territorial divisions.

questions.prompt: Which station was warmer that day?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented one-day readings: West station 12°C and 18 mm rain; East station 14°C and 4 mm. In the UK, west-facing high ground often receives more rain.
questions.model: 14°C is warmer than 12°C.

questions.prompt: How many respondents enjoy both activities?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented town survey: 12 people enjoy football, 8 enjoy music and 5 enjoy both. These are separate overlapping groups, not national statistics.
questions.model: The source states an overlap of five.

lines: Which pair belongs on a physical layer?
Give one short answer when invited.

A country boundary marks a territorial division; a ridge describes elevated land. They may coincide but need not. A map key should use different symbols so a reader does not mistake every border for a mountain.
questions.model: Rivers and uplands. Physical layers describe landscape features; political layers describe territorial organisation.

lines: The incoming air becomes much drier. What prediction follows, other things equal?
Give one short answer when invited.

Moist air rises over high ground and cools. Condensation can form cloud and precipitation. Descending air on the other side may be drier; wind and moisture supply matter, so a mountain does not guarantee rain every day.
questions.model: Less moisture is available for precipitation. Cooling changes conditions for condensation; it does not create water.

lines: Eight swim, six run and three do both; everyone does at least one. How many people?
Give one short answer when invited.
Of 10 walkers and 7 cyclists, 4 do both. Put 4 in the overlap, then 6 walkers only and 3 cyclists only: total 13. Adding 10 and 7 without subtracting the overlap counts four people twice.
questions.model: 11. 8 + 6 - 3 = 11 distinct people.

lines: Which two features are physical?
Map layers: country boundary for Wales; approximate upland area labelled Scottish Highlands; river line labelled Thames. A city point is also marked. Colours and symbols are explained in the key.
questions.model: Scottish Highlands and Thames: relief and a river, rather than a country boundary.

lines: Which station is wetter, and by how much?
Fictional weather on one day: West station 24°C and 28 mm rain; East station 27°C and 2 mm rain. A mountain stands between them. Incoming air is moist and blows from the west.
questions.model: West has 26 mm more rain that day.

lines: How many like walking, including those who like both?
Fictional club survey: 19 pupils like walking only, 15 like cycling only, 16 like both. Everyone surveyed likes at least one. The survey was conducted at an outdoor club.
questions.model: 19+16=35. “Walking” is not the same as “walking only”.

lines: Which layer would help investigate high land?
Map layers: country boundary for Wales; approximate upland area labelled Scottish Highlands; river line labelled Thames. A city point is also marked. Colours and symbols are explained in the key.
questions.model: Relief or elevation information. Country colour alone does not show height.

lines: Does this one day establish the climate?
Fictional weather on one day: West station 24°C and 28 mm rain; East station 27°C and 2 mm rain. A mountain stands between them. Incoming air is moist and blows from the west.
questions.model: No. Climate needs long-term patterns, not one day’s weather.

lines: Can this show what every pupil at school prefers?
Fictional club survey: 19 pupils like walking only, 15 like cycling only, 16 like both. Everyone surveyed likes at least one. The survey was conducted at an outdoor club.
questions.model: No. Outdoor-club respondents may not represent all pupils.

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented maps: A has houses around a crossroads; B has houses along a road; C has widely separated farms.
questions.model: B follows a line along a road.

lines: Homes form a long row beside one road. Which label fits the pattern?
Give one short answer when invited.

A cluster around a junction is nucleated; a row along a road is linear; isolated farms are dispersed. First describe locations. A road may influence development, but the drawing alone cannot prove residents' reasons.
questions.model: Linear. The buildings follow a line rather than being scattered independently.

lines: Which visible feature makes B linear?
Fictional plans: A has homes around a crossroads; B has homes in a row along a road; C has separated farms among fields. Later, 4 new homes are built beside the road through C.
questions.model: Buildings follow a line along the road.

lines: After the new homes, must all of C be called linear?
Fictional plans: A has homes around a crossroads; B has homes in a row along a road; C has separated farms among fields. Later, 4 new homes are built beside the road through C.
questions.model: No. New linear development and older dispersed farms can coexist.

questions.prompt: Which town has higher average income?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented towns: A has average income 30 tokens and 10-minute clinic access; B has 40 tokens and 45-minute clinic access.
questions.model: Forty exceeds thirty.

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Examples of London functions: Parliament for government; museums for culture; stations for transport. A city can serve residents and visitors.
questions.model: London lies on the Thames.

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented journey: a UK shop buys fruit from another country; visitors travel to the UK; a class exchanges messages with an overseas class.
questions.model: Messages communicate information.

lines: A new clinic cuts average travel time. What can be concluded directly?
Give one short answer when invited.

If clinic travel drops from 40 to 15 minutes, access improves by 25 minutes. It does not follow that housing, air quality or every resident's health improved. Change the specific claim and retain the unknowns.
questions.model: Average access time improved. One improved indicator does not establish every outcome for every person.

lines: Which arrow label explains a city connection?
Give one short answer when invited.

A station connects travellers to offices, museums and services. Draw an arrow labelled “carries workers” rather than just “link”. A useful network explains what moves, between which places, and why it matters.
questions.model: Bus route carries visitors from station to museum. The first names the movement and its function.

lines: Which response directly moves goods around a closed port?
Give one short answer when invited.

If a port closes, a new sea route, stored supplies or reduced demand may help in different ways. Identify what is interrupted first. A working internet connection cannot physically replace a delayed food shipment.
questions.model: Use another available port and compare added cost. Information can coordinate action, but goods need a usable physical route.

lines: Which offers the shorter clinic journey?

Fictional neighbourhood A: average income 110 tokens, clinic 10 minutes away, no park. B: average income 125, clinic 35 minutes away, park nearby. These are averages and travel estimates, not descriptions of every resident.
questions.model: A by 25 minutes. A person needing frequent care may value this strongly.

lines: Explain one connection between functions.

Fictional city network: homes connect to a station, museum, council office and market. Today the station is closed. A group needs travel to work. No alternative timetable or access report has been supplied.
questions.model: Transport may help people reach work, services or cultural sites. Name both ends and what moves.

lines: From the receiving country’s view, what are the same goods?
Fictional trade: bicycles move from Country C to Country D. Payment moves back. An order message travels online. A worker separately travels to visit relatives. A port then closes.
questions.model: An import into Country D. The movement has not changed, only the viewpoint.

lines: New clinic cuts B’s journey to 12 minutes. What changes?

Fictional neighbourhood A: average income 110 tokens, clinic 10 minutes away, no park. B: average income 125, clinic 35 minutes away, park nearby. These are averages and travel estimates, not descriptions of every resident.
questions.model: The access gap shrinks to 2 minutes. Other differences and people’s needs remain.

lines: Can a city still function when one facility closes?

Fictional city network: homes connect to a station, museum, council office and market. Today the station is closed. A group needs travel to work. No alternative timetable or access report has been supplied.
questions.model: Often other links exist, but the source does not confirm their availability. Investigate alternatives.

lines: Does a port closure automatically stop online messages?
Fictional trade: bicycles move from Country C to Country D. Payment moves back. An order message travels online. A worker separately travels to visit relatives. A port then closes.
questions.model: No. Different flows can use different networks.

Use another available port and compare added cost. Information can coordinate action, but goods need a usable physical route.
A by 25 minutes. A person needing frequent care may value this strongly.
Transport may help people reach work, services or cultural sites. Name both ends and what moves.
An import into Country D. The movement has not changed, only the viewpoint.
The access gap shrinks to 2 minutes. Other differences and people’s needs remain.
Often other links exist, but the source does not confirm their availability. Investigate alternatives.
No. Different flows can use different networks.

questions.prompt: Which town has higher average income?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented towns: A has average income 30 tokens and 10-minute clinic access; B has 40 tokens and 45-minute clinic access.
questions.model: Forty exceeds thirty.

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Examples of London functions: Parliament for government; museums for culture; stations for transport. A city can serve residents and visitors.
questions.model: London lies on the Thames.

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented journey: a UK shop buys fruit from another country; visitors travel to the UK; a class exchanges messages with an overseas class.
questions.model: Messages communicate information.

lines: A new clinic cuts average travel time. What can be concluded directly?
Give one short answer when invited.

If clinic travel drops from 40 to 15 minutes, access improves by 25 minutes. It does not follow that housing, air quality or every resident's health improved. Change the specific claim and retain the unknowns.
questions.model: Average access time improved. One improved indicator does not establish every outcome for every person.

lines: Which arrow label explains a city connection?
Give one short answer when invited.

A station connects travellers to offices, museums and services. Draw an arrow labelled “carries workers” rather than just “link”. A useful network explains what moves, between which places, and why it matters.
questions.model: Bus route carries visitors from station to museum. The first names the movement and its function.

lines: Which response directly moves goods around a closed port?
Give one short answer when invited.

If a port closes, a new sea route, stored supplies or reduced demand may help in different ways. Identify what is interrupted first. A working internet connection cannot physically replace a delayed food shipment.
questions.model: Use another available port and compare added cost. Information can coordinate action, but goods need a usable physical route.

lines: Which offers the shorter clinic journey?

Fictional neighbourhood A: average income 140 tokens, clinic 10 minutes away, no park. B: average income 155, clinic 35 minutes away, park nearby. These are averages and travel estimates, not descriptions of every resident.
questions.model: A by 25 minutes. A person needing frequent care may value this strongly.

lines: Explain one connection between functions.

Fictional city network: homes connect to a station, museum, council office and market. Today the station is closed. A group needs travel to work. No alternative timetable or access report has been supplied.
questions.model: Transport may help people reach work, services or cultural sites. Name both ends and what moves.

lines: From the receiving country’s view, what are the same goods?
Fictional trade: bicycles move from Country C to Country D. Payment moves back. An order message travels online. A worker separately travels to visit relatives. A port then closes.
questions.model: An import into Country D. The movement has not changed, only the viewpoint.

lines: New clinic cuts B’s journey to 12 minutes. What changes?

Fictional neighbourhood A: average income 140 tokens, clinic 10 minutes away, no park. B: average income 155, clinic 35 minutes away, park nearby. These are averages and travel estimates, not descriptions of every resident.
questions.model: The access gap shrinks to 2 minutes. Other differences and people’s needs remain.

lines: Can a city still function when one facility closes?

Fictional city network: homes connect to a station, museum, council office and market. Today the station is closed. A group needs travel to work. No alternative timetable or access report has been supplied.
questions.model: Often other links exist, but the source does not confirm their availability. Investigate alternatives.

lines: Does a port closure automatically stop online messages?
Fictional trade: bicycles move from Country C to Country D. Payment moves back. An order message travels online. A worker separately travels to visit relatives. A port then closes.
questions.model: No. Different flows can use different networks.

lines: Which offers the shorter clinic journey?

Fictional neighbourhood A: average income 150 tokens, clinic 10 minutes away, no park. B: average income 165, clinic 35 minutes away, park nearby. These are averages and travel estimates, not descriptions of every resident.

lines: Explain one connection between functions.

lines: From the receiving country’s view, what are the same goods?

lines: New clinic cuts B’s journey to 12 minutes. What changes?

lines: Can a city still function when one facility closes?

lines: Which revision is justified by a valley photograph alone?
Give one short answer when invited.

“Ice covered this place exactly 12,000 years ago” includes extent and date. A photograph of a valley shape does not establish either precisely. Ask for deposit mapping, dating and evidence of ice movement.
questions.model: The shape is consistent with past glacial erosion; more evidence is needed. Qualify an interpretation when the evidence does not establish timing or extent.

lines: Which part is an interpretation?

questions.prompt: What is the first year's balance?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Practice glacier: snowfall adds 9 units of ice-equivalent mass in a year; melting removes 6 units. This is an invented mass balance.
questions.model: Nine minus six gives a gain of three.

lines: Additions are 6 units and losses 9. What is the balance?
Give one short answer when invited.
If additions are 8 units and losses 5, the store gains 3. If the next year adds 4 and loses 6, it loses 2; the two-year net gain is 1. Balance is additions minus losses, not their sum.
questions.model: -3 units. Losses exceed additions by 3, reducing the ice store.

lines: Find the store after Year 1.
Fictional glacier store starts at 35 units. Year 1 adds 7 and loses 4. Year 2 adds 3 and loses 7. Ice continues to flow downhill while these gains and losses occur.

Plucking removes blocks loosened from bedrock; transport carries debris; abrasion occurs when debris held by moving ice scrapes the bed.
Label each action separately so “erosion” does not hide the mechanism.

cards.front: Which process makes scratches with rock carried by ice?
cards.back: Debris scrapes the surface as ice moves.
Rock fragments carried in ice scrape bedrock. Moving debris can wear and scratch rock surfaces.
Ice removes a loosened block from the bed or side.
Deposition: the carried material is left behind.

questions.prompt: Which section best matches a glacial trough?

lines: Which view best shows a valley's U-shaped cross-section?
Give one short answer when invited.

Draw the valley as if sliced across. River erosion can form a narrow V; glacial erosion can widen the floor and steepen sides into a trough. Arrows should point at the surfaces removed, not imply ice deposits the valley.
questions.model: A slice across the valley. Cross-section displays floor width and side slopes directly.

lines: Which view shows floor width and side slopes?
Cross-section A has sides meeting at a narrow V-shaped bottom. B has a broad floor and steep sides. A plan view shows the valley bending east.
questions.model: A cross-section cuts across the valley.

lines: Does “U-shaped” mean the valley follows a U on a map?
Cross-section A has sides meeting at a narrow V-shaped bottom. B has a broad floor and steep sides. A plan view shows the valley bending east.

questions.model: Deposition lays material down.

lines: Why can a direct ice deposit contain mixed sizes?
Give one short answer when invited.

Ice can carry particles of many sizes together. As it melts, debris may be released as unsorted till; a moraine is an accumulation of glacial debris. Contrast deposition with the earlier removal and transport.
questions.model: Ice can carry and release fine and coarse debris together. Direct deposition by ice need not sort particles like flowing meltwater can.

lines: Why is material left at the melting margin?
An invented ice margin retreats, leaving mixed clay, gravel and boulders. A nearby stream later sorts some debris by size.
questions.model: The ice releases its load as it melts: deposition.

lines: A boulder lies beyond today’s ice edge. Must the glacier never have reached it?
An invented ice margin retreats, leaving mixed clay, gravel and boulders. A nearby stream later sorts some debris by size.
questions.model: No. A former margin may have extended farther, though other evidence is needed to establish its history.

questions.prompt: Which material is typical of till?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Practice deposit: clay, sand, pebbles and boulders lie mixed together beside a former glacier. A ridge of debris follows its old edge.
questions.model: Till is commonly unsorted glacial debris.

lines: Which evidence strengthens a former-ice-margin interpretation?
Give one short answer when invited.

A debris ridge may mark a former ice margin, but first check its material, shape and relation to other glacial evidence. Draw a possible ice outline with a dashed line to show the inference is provisional.
questions.model: Ridge material and position consistent with surrounding glacial features. Composition and spatial context help distinguish possible origins.

lines: Why is material left at the melting margin?
A fictional glacier carries debris down-valley. At a melting margin, mixed material is released. Later water moves the smaller grains.
questions.model: The ice releases its load as it melts: deposition.

lines: A boulder lies beyond today’s ice edge. Must the glacier never have reached it?
A fictional glacier carries debris down-valley. At a melting margin, mixed material is released. Later water moves the smaller grains.
questions.model: No. A former margin may have extended farther, though other evidence is needed to establish its history.

questions.prompt: Which shape is associated with a glacial valley?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Case note: Langdale is a Lake District glacial valley. Practice visitor counts: path A 80 and path B 20 in one hour; these counts are invented.
questions.model: Ice can form broad U-shaped valleys.

lines: Which pair best tests whether heavy use is affecting a path?
Give one short answer when invited.

A glacial trough's scenery can attract visitors, but visitor numbers alone do not measure damage. Compare counts alongside path width, bare ground and repeated observations. Design a test before prescribing a response.
questions.model: Repeated visitor counts and path-condition measurements. Pressure and condition must both be measured over comparable observations.

lines: Which measure describes pressure, and which describes condition?
Fictional valley paths: A 80 visitors/hour, B 25. Bare-ground width is 3 m on A and 1 m on B. A proposal redirects 20 visitors/hour from A to B. No safe capacity is known.
questions.model: Visitor count measures use pressure; bare-ground width measures a condition of the path.

lines: Will moving visitors automatically solve the problem?
Fictional valley paths: A 80 visitors/hour, B 25. Bare-ground width is 3 m on A and 1 m on B. A proposal redirects 20 visitors/hour from A to B. No safe capacity is known.
questions.model: No. B may be sensitive or lack capacity. Monitor both routes.

lines: Why is “more melt now means more water forever” weak?
Give one short answer when invited.

More melt may increase release now while reducing the stored ice available later. A bank account analogy helps: a larger withdrawal today does not prove a larger future balance. Actual runoff also depends on precipitation and season.
questions.model: It ignores depletion of the ice store and other water inputs. A short-term flow increase does not establish a permanent supply increase.

lines: Two streams join. What is the meeting point called?
Give one short answer when invited.

A tributary joins the main river at a confluence. The source begins the river; the mouth is where it enters another water body. Follow the arrows downstream instead of treating every branching line as a river splitting.
questions.model: A confluence. A confluence is a junction; a watershed is a drainage divide.

lines: After rainfall, must all water reach the river immediately?
Give one short answer when invited.

One drop runs over the surface into a stream; another infiltrates and may move slowly through soil and rock. Storage and pathway affect timing. Water does not follow one fixed loop at one universal speed.
questions.model: No; some infiltrates or remains in stores. Different pathways and stores produce different travel times.

lines: How much water left the store during that period?
Fictional glacier water store: starts 330 units; gains 33; loses 38. A second period has the same gain but 5 extra units lost. These are model units, not a forecast.
questions.model: 38 units. Outflow is different from the amount remaining.

lines: What is a tributary?
Fictional route: two upland streams meet above a village; the combined river flows south to the sea. A road crosses downstream of the village.
questions.model: A smaller stream or river joining another river.

lines: Name the formation of liquid droplets from water vapour.
A fictional water-cycle model follows water from a lake into air, then a cloud, rain, soil and a stream. Some water remains stored underground.
questions.model: Condensation. Cloud droplets do not form because water disappears.

lines: Why can more release now mean less stored water later?
Fictional glacier water store: starts 330 units; gains 33; loses 38. A second period has the same gain but 5 extra units lost. These are model units, not a forecast.
questions.model: A larger loss drains the finite store faster unless gains increase enough to replace it.

lines: Where is the mouth?
Fictional route: two upland streams meet above a village; the combined river flows south to the sea. A road crosses downstream of the village.
questions.model: Where the river enters the sea or another receiving water body.

lines: What is infiltration?
A fictional water-cycle model follows water from a lake into air, then a cloud, rain, soil and a stream. Some water remains stored underground.

questions.prompt: Which group may depend on downstream water?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented mountain community: summer meltwater supports a river. A changing glacier may alter when water arrives. No future flow figures are supplied.

options.label: Only people who never use water

questions.model: River water may support agriculture.

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
The Thames flows through southern England and London towards the North Sea through its estuary. Practice route: spring → small stream → town → estuary.
questions.model: The source is the river's beginning.

questions.prompt: Which process takes water into soil?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Practice sequence: sunlight warms a lake; water vapour cools into droplets; rain falls; water flows over or enters soil.
questions.model: Infiltration moves water into the ground.

lines: Why is “more melt now means more water forever” weak?
Give one short answer when invited.

More melt may increase release now while reducing the stored ice available later. A bank account analogy helps: a larger withdrawal today does not prove a larger future balance. Actual runoff also depends on precipitation and season.
questions.model: It ignores depletion of the ice store and other water inputs. A short-term flow increase does not establish a permanent supply increase.

lines: Two streams join. What is the meeting point called?
Give one short answer when invited.

A tributary joins the main river at a confluence. The source begins the river; the mouth is where it enters another water body. Follow the arrows downstream instead of treating every branching line as a river splitting.
questions.model: A confluence. A confluence is a junction; a watershed is a drainage divide.

lines: After rainfall, must all water reach the river immediately?
Give one short answer when invited.

One drop runs over the surface into a stream; another infiltrates and may move slowly through soil and rock. Storage and pathway affect timing. Water does not follow one fixed loop at one universal speed.
questions.model: No; some infiltrates or remains in stores. Different pathways and stores produce different travel times.

lines: How much water left the store during that period?
Fictional glacier water store: starts 390 units; gains 39; loses 44. A second period has the same gain but 5 extra units lost. These are model units, not a forecast.
questions.model: 44 units. Outflow is different from the amount remaining.

lines: What is a tributary?
Fictional route: two upland streams meet above a village; the combined river flows south to the sea. A road crosses downstream of the village.
questions.model: A smaller stream or river joining another river.

lines: Name the formation of liquid droplets from water vapour.
A fictional water-cycle model follows water from a lake into air, then a cloud, rain, soil and a stream. Some water remains stored underground.
questions.model: Condensation. Cloud droplets do not form because water disappears.

lines: Why can more release now mean less stored water later?
Fictional glacier water store: starts 390 units; gains 39; loses 44. A second period has the same gain but 5 extra units lost. These are model units, not a forecast.
questions.model: A larger loss drains the finite store faster unless gains increase enough to replace it.

lines: Where is the mouth?
Fictional route: two upland streams meet above a village; the combined river flows south to the sea. A road crosses downstream of the village.
questions.model: Where the river enters the sea or another receiving water body.

lines: What is infiltration?
A fictional water-cycle model follows water from a lake into air, then a cloud, rain, soil and a stream. Some water remains stored underground.
questions.model: Water entering the soil from the surface.

cards.front: Which process takes water into soil?

A confluence. A confluence is a junction; a watershed is a drainage divide.

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented mountain community: summer meltwater supports a river. A changing glacier may alter when water arrives. No future flow figures are supplied.

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
The Thames flows through southern England and London towards the North Sea through its estuary. Practice route: spring → small stream → town → estuary.

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.

lines: Start 50, add 4, lose 9. What is the final store?
Give one short answer when invited.
A store starting at 40 units, gaining 7 and losing 10, ends at 37. Separate stored water from water released this period. Model units illustrate a balance, not an actual glacier forecast.
questions.model: 45 units. 50 + 4 - 9 = 45; losses leave the store.

lines: A pollutant enters at B on A → B → C. Which place is downstream?
Give one short answer when invited.
In a model A → B → C, a release at B travels towards C, not upstream to A. This establishes direction, not exact arrival time. Real timing needs flow speed, distance, mixing and other evidence.
questions.model: C. Follow the indicated flow direction; a precise warning time needs more data.

lines: Which process turns water vapour into liquid droplets?
Give one short answer when invited.

Evaporation changes liquid to vapour using energy; condensation changes vapour to liquid droplets. Precipitation moves water down from the atmosphere. Give each arrow its own process name rather than calling every movement evaporation.
questions.model: Condensation. Condensation changes state; infiltration is water entering the ground.

lines: How much water left the store during that period?
Fictional glacier water store: starts 410 units; gains 41; loses 46. A second period has the same gain but 5 extra units lost. These are model units, not a forecast.
questions.model: 46 units. Outflow is different from the amount remaining.

lines: What is a tributary?
Fictional route: two upland streams meet above a village; the combined river flows south to the sea. A road crosses downstream of the village.
questions.model: A smaller stream or river joining another river.

lines: Name the formation of liquid droplets from water vapour.
A fictional water-cycle model follows water from a lake into air, then a cloud, rain, soil and a stream. Some water remains stored underground.
questions.model: Condensation. Cloud droplets do not form because water disappears.

lines: Why can more release now mean less stored water later?
Fictional glacier water store: starts 410 units; gains 41; loses 46. A second period has the same gain but 5 extra units lost. These are model units, not a forecast.
questions.model: A larger loss drains the finite store faster unless gains increase enough to replace it.

lines: Where is the mouth?
Fictional route: two upland streams meet above a village; the combined river flows south to the sea. A road crosses downstream of the village.
questions.model: Where the river enters the sea or another receiving water body.

lines: What is infiltration?
A fictional water-cycle model follows water from a lake into air, then a cloud, rain, soil and a stream. Some water remains stored underground.
questions.model: Water entering the soil from the surface.

cards.back: Glacier ice stores freshwater.
A tributary joins a larger stream or river.
Condensation changes vapour into liquid.
45 units. 50 + 4 - 9 = 45; losses leave the store.
C. Follow the indicated flow direction; a precise warning time needs more data.
Condensation. Condensation changes state; infiltration is water entering the ground.
46 units. Outflow is different from the amount remaining.
A smaller stream or river joining another river.
Condensation. Cloud droplets do not form because water disappears.
A larger loss drains the finite store faster unless gains increase enough to replace it.
Where the river enters the sea or another receiving water body.
Water entering the soil from the surface.

lines: Rain falls on opposite sides of a ridge separating two basins. What may happen?

A drainage basin is land draining to an outlet. A watershed divides neighbouring basins; rain falling on opposite sides may enter different streams. The divide is not the river itself.

questions.model: Yes. Its surface drainage may go into the neighbouring basin.

lines: What must happen before a bend becomes an isolated oxbow lake?
Give one short answer when invited.

A meander neck narrows, a shorter channel breaks through and deposition can isolate the old bend as an oxbow lake. For a waterfall, undercutting and collapse can move the fall upstream, leaving a gorge behind.
questions.model: A new channel bypasses the bend and the old entrances become blocked. Cut-off and isolation explain the feature; it is not merely a circular river on a map.

lines: What happens after collapse?
A fictional waterfall undercuts a softer layer beneath a resistant ledge. The overhang collapses, and repeated retreat leaves a steep-sided gorge.

lines: Does the diagram give the exact speed of retreat?
A fictional waterfall undercuts a softer layer beneath a resistant ledge. The overhang collapses, and repeated retreat leaves a steep-sided gorge.

questions.prompt: Which is an impact rather than a cause?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented catchments receive equal rain. A has wet soil and many paved surfaces; B has drier soil and more permeable ground.
questions.model: Damage is a consequence of flooding.

lines: Which item is an impact rather than a cause of flooding?
Give one short answer when invited.
Heavy rain on saturated soil may increase rapid runoff; flow exceeding channel capacity may flood homes. “Wet weather → damage” skips the mechanism. Separate the cause, pathway and consequence.
questions.model: Homes damaged by floodwater. Damage is a consequence; rainfall contributes to the water input.

lines: Calculate infiltration and runoff for B.
Fictional runoff model: rain 40 units. Surface A allows 50% to infiltrate; B allows 20%. All remaining water is counted as runoff. The model omits storage, evaporation and timing.

lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.

questions.prompt: What hazard is the Thames Barrier designed to help manage?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Thames case principle: the Thames Barrier helps protect London from tidal surges. Invented flood log: 10 homes flooded, one road closed, repairs lasted four weeks.
questions.model: It is part of tidal flood protection.

lines: A local drain is blocked after rain. What directly addresses that blockage?
Give one short answer when invited.

A tidal barrier addresses incoming high water at its protected location; it does not remove every upstream rainfall or drainage problem. Warnings help preparation, while drainage work addresses a different pathway.
questions.model: Appropriate drainage maintenance. Measures have different mechanisms and geographical coverage.

lines: Name two immediate impacts.

Fictional event log: heavy rain on saturated ground; river overflow; 12 homes flooded; road closed for 4 days; warnings issued; repairs continued afterwards. This is not a historical report about a named flood.
questions.model: 12 flooded homes and the road closure. Keep impacts separate from the rain itself.

lines: What may continue after water recedes?

questions.prompt: What can a warning system do?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented budget 60: warning system 10; restore wetland 40; flood wall 80. A warning helps people respond but does not stop water.
questions.model: Warnings support action but do not stop water.

lines: Two packages both fit the budget. What should decide the recommendation next?
Give one short answer when invited.

A higher budget creates options but does not establish the best one. Compare which flood mechanism each measure addresses, who benefits, maintenance and environmental effects. State an evidence need before committing to a recommendation.
questions.model: Suitability and effects supported by local evidence. Cost is a constraint and trade-off, not a complete measure of effectiveness.

lines: Can warnings and storage be combined?

Fictional flood options: warnings 10 tokens; storage area 40; wall 80. Budget 80. Warnings help people respond; storage may hold water at a suitable site; a wall can block flow locally but may transfer risk.
questions.model: Yes: 10+40=50 tokens, leaving 30.

lines: Budget rises to 100. Compare two possible packages.

Fictional flood options: warnings 10 tokens; storage area 40; wall 80. Budget 80. Warnings help people respond; storage may hold water at a suitable site; a wall can block flow locally but may transfer risk.
questions.model: Warnings + wall = 90; warnings + storage = 50. Explain different functions and limits, not just price.

questions.prompt: Which is an impact rather than a cause?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented catchments receive equal rain. A has wet soil and many paved surfaces; B has drier soil and more permeable ground.
questions.model: Damage is a consequence of flooding.

questions.prompt: Which impact lasted beyond the flood day?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Thames case principle: the Thames Barrier helps protect London from tidal surges. Invented flood log: 10 homes flooded, one road closed, repairs lasted four weeks.
questions.model: Repairs continued after the event.

questions.prompt: What can a warning system do?
lines: Choose an answer. Explain your reason.
Invented budget 60: warning system 10; restore wetland 40; flood wall 80. A warning helps people respond but does not stop water.
questions.model: Warnings support action but do not stop water.

lines: Which item is an impact rather than a cause of flooding?
Give one short answer when invited.
Heavy rain on saturated soil may increase rapid runoff; flow exceeding channel capacity may flood homes. “Wet weather → damage” skips the mechanism. Separate the cause, pathway and consequence.
questions.model: Homes damaged by floodwater. Damage is a consequence; rainfall contributes to the water input.

lines: An invented exercise says 12 homes flooded. How should it be reported?
Give one short answer when invited.

Sort a fictional event into trigger, mechanism, impacts and responses. Label dates and counts by their source. An invented classroom log can practise reasoning but must not become a claimed historical Thames event.
questions.model: As a figure from the fictional exercise. Source identity is part of accurate case-study reporting.

lines: Two packages both fit the budget. What should decide the recommendation next?
Give one short answer when invited.

A higher budget creates options but does not establish the best one. Compare which flood mechanism each measure addresses, who benefits, maintenance and environmental effects. State an evidence need before committing to a recommendation.
questions.model: Suitability and effects supported by local evidence. Cost is a constraint and trade-off, not a complete measure of effectiveness.

lines: Calculate infiltration and runoff for B.
Fictional runoff model: rain 430 units. Surface A allows 50% to infiltrate; B allows 20%. All remaining water is counted as runoff. The model omits storage, evaporation and timing.
questions.model: 86 infiltrates; 344 runs off.

lines: Name two immediate impacts.

Fictional event log: heavy rain on saturated ground; river overflow; 88 homes flooded; road closed for 42 days; warnings issued; repairs continued afterwards. This is not a historical report about a named flood.
questions.model: 88 flooded homes and the road closure. Keep impacts separate from the rain itself.

lines: Can warnings and storage be combined?

Fictional flood options: warnings 10 tokens; storage area 40; wall 80. Budget 470. Warnings help people respond; storage may hold water at a suitable site; a wall can block flow locally but may transfer risk.
questions.model: Yes: 10+40=50 tokens, leaving 420.

lines: Double the rain while keeping the percentages. What happens?
Fictional runoff model: rain 430 units. Surface A allows 50% to infiltrate; B allows 20%. All remaining water is counted as runoff. The model omits storage, evaporation and timing.
questions.model: Both model quantities double. The simplified model keeps the proportions fixed.

lines: What may continue after water recedes?

Fictional event log: heavy rain on saturated ground; river overflow; 88 homes flooded; road closed for 42 days; warnings issued; repairs continued afterwards. This is not a historical report about a named flood.
questions.model: Repairs, disrupted journeys or loss of use of buildings. Use the log without inventing measured costs.

lines: Budget rises to 100. Compare two possible packages.

Fictional flood options: warnings 10 tokens; storage area 40; wall 80. Budget 470. Warnings help people respond; storage may hold water at a suitable site; a wall can block flow locally but may transfer risk.
questions.model: Warnings + wall = 90; warnings + storage = 50. Explain different functions and limits, not just price.

blocks.title: Retrieval beats rereading
lines: Read the notes from your recent lessons. Close them and explain three ideas from memory.
Practise a question, check the explanation, and correct your reasoning.
